title: Degrees, Levels, and Profiles of Contextuality
summary: We introduce a new notion, that of a contextuality profile of a system. Rather than characterizing a system's contextuality by a single number, its overall degree of contextuality, we show how it can be characterized by a curve relating degree of contextuality to level at which the system is considered,\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \textnormal{level} & 1 & \cdots & n-1 & n>1 & n+1 & \cdots & N\\ \hline \textnormal{degree} & 0 & \cdots & 0 & d_{n}>0 & d_{n+1}\geq d_{n} & \cdots & d_{N}\geq d_{N-1} \end{array},where N is the maximum number of variables per system's context. A system is represented at level n if one only considers the joint distributions with k\leq n variables, ignoring higher-order joint distributions. We show that the level-wise contextuality analysis can be used in conjunction with any well-constructed measure of contextuality. We present a method of concatenated systems to explore contextuality profiles systematically, and we apply it to the contextuality profiles for three major measures of contextuality proposed in the literature.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces contextuality profiles as curves showing how a system's degree of contextuality varies with the level of joint distributions considered, rather than using a single overall measure.
AI.motivation: Current approaches characterize system contextuality with a single number (overall degree), but this fails to capture how contextuality manifests at different levels of analysis when considering joint distributions of varying numbers of variables.
AI.method: Introduces contextuality profiles as curves relating degree of contextuality to level n (number of variables per context considered). Develops method of concatenated systems to systematically explore these profiles and applies it to three major contextuality measures from literature.
AI.result: Shows that systems can be represented at different levels by considering only joint distributions with k ≤ n variables, ignoring higher-order distributions. Demonstrates that level-wise contextuality analysis works with any well-constructed contextuality measure.
AI.conclusion: Contextuality profiles provide a more nuanced characterization of system contextuality than single-number measures, revealing how contextuality emerges at different levels of analysis and enabling systematic exploration through concatenated systems.

title: Quantum Fuzzy Sets Revisited: Density Matrices, Decoherence, and the Q-Matrix Framework
summary: In 2006 we proposed Quantum Fuzzy Sets, observing that states of a quantum register could serve as characteristic functions of fuzzy subsets, embedding Zadeh's unit interval into the Bloch sphere. That paper was deliberately preliminary. In the two decades since, the idea has been taken up by researchers working on quantum annealers, intuitionistic fuzzy connectives, and quantum machine learning, while parallel developments in categorical quantum mechanics have reshaped the theoretical landscape. The present paper revisits that programme and introduces two main extensions. First, we move from pure states to density matrices, so that truth values occupy the entire Bloch ball rather than its surface; this captures the phenomenon of semantic decoherence that pure-state semantics cannot express. Second, we introduce the Q-Matrix, a global density matrix from which individual quantum fuzzy sets emerge as local sections via partial trace. We define a category QFS of quantum fuzzy sets, establish basic structural properties (monoidal structure, fibration over Set), characterize the classical limit as simultaneous diagonalizability, and exhibit an obstruction to a fully internal Frobenius-algebra treatment.

AI.tldr: Quantum Fuzzy Sets extended from pure states to density matrices, introducing Q-Matrix for global representation and semantic decoherence, with categorical framework QFS.
AI.motivation: To revisit and extend the 2006 Quantum Fuzzy Sets proposal by addressing limitations of pure-state semantics and incorporating developments in quantum computing and categorical quantum mechanics over two decades.
AI.method: 1) Extend from pure states to density matrices (Bloch ball instead of sphere) to capture semantic decoherence; 2) Introduce Q-Matrix as global density matrix from which individual quantum fuzzy sets emerge via partial trace; 3) Define category QFS of quantum fuzzy sets with structural analysis.
AI.result: Established monoidal structure and fibration over Set for QFS category, characterized classical limit as simultaneous diagonalizability, and identified obstruction to fully internal Frobenius-algebra treatment.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive extension of Quantum Fuzzy Sets theory that incorporates density matrices for semantic decoherence and establishes a categorical framework, addressing limitations of the original pure-state approach while connecting to contemporary quantum computing developments.

title: Resurgence Theory and Holomorphic Quantum Mechanics
summary: In this work, we study the resurgence program in holomorphic quantum mechanics. As a specific problem, we investigate the resurgence in the quartic anharmonic oscillator within holomorphic quantum mechanics, using the Bargmann representation of bosonic operators. In this framework, the perturbative energy series is shown to be Gevrey-1 and Borel summable only after continuation across the Stokes line. The instanton operator, realized as a coherent-state displacement in the Segal--Bargmann space, provides an explicit operatorial bridge between perturbative coefficients and non-perturbative sectors. Alien derivative relations generate the full resurgence triangle characteristic of the Bender--Wu model, and the resummed energy is expressed as a trans-series via a ratio of expectation values involving this instanton operator. As a concrete demonstration, we compute the first seven energy levels ($n=0,\dots,6$) up to sixth order in the coupling $g$; the resulting exact rational coefficients reproduce the classic Bender--Wu results, confirming the consistency and power of the holomorphic resurgence approach.

AI.tldr: Holomorphic quantum mechanics framework applied to quartic anharmonic oscillator reveals Borel summability after Stokes line crossing, with instanton operator connecting perturbative and non-perturbative sectors, reproducing Bender-Wu results.
AI.motivation: To investigate resurgence phenomena in quantum mechanics using holomorphic methods, specifically studying how perturbative expansions relate to non-perturbative effects in the quartic anharmonic oscillator.
AI.method: Uses Bargmann representation of bosonic operators within holomorphic quantum mechanics framework. Implements instanton operator as coherent-state displacement in Segal-Bargmann space. Applies alien derivative relations to generate resurgence triangle structure. Computes energy levels via trans-series expressed as ratio of expectation values involving instanton operator.
AI.result: Perturbative energy series is Gevrey-1 and Borel summable only after continuation across Stokes line. Full resurgence triangle characteristic of Bender-Wu model generated. First seven energy levels (n=0,...,6) computed up to sixth order in coupling g, reproducing exact rational coefficients from classic Bender-Wu results.
AI.conclusion: The holomorphic resurgence approach provides consistent and powerful framework for connecting perturbative and non-perturbative sectors in quantum mechanics, with instanton operator serving as explicit operatorial bridge between these regimes.

title: Approximate Error Correction for Quantum Simulations of SU(2) Lattice Gauge Theories
summary: We present a protocol for actively suppressing Gauss law violations in quantum simulations of SU(2) lattice gauge theory. The protocol uses mid-circuit measurements to extract a characterization of the gauge-violation sector at each lattice vertex, resolving both the total angular momentum and magnetic quantum numbers of the violation via a group quantum Fourier transform. Syndrome-conditional recovery operations map the state back to the gauge-invariant subspace through an iterative sweep over vertices, a procedure we call gauge cooling. We show that while the Knill-Laflamme conditions are not generically satisfied at vertices with nontrivial singlet multiplicity, every single-qubit error is detected by the gauge syndrome. We demonstrate gauge cooling on a single-plaquette simulation of the Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian truncated to the spin-$1/2$ representation under depolarizing and amplitude damping noise, showing that the protocol restores gauge invariance and improves fidelity at noise rates representative of current superconducting hardware.

AI.tldr: Protocol for suppressing gauge law violations in quantum simulations of SU(2) lattice gauge theory using mid-circuit measurements and syndrome-conditional recovery operations.
AI.motivation: Quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories suffer from gauge law violations due to hardware noise; active suppression is needed to maintain gauge invariance and improve simulation fidelity.
AI.method: Uses mid-circuit measurements with group quantum Fourier transform to extract gauge-violation syndrome at each vertex, followed by iterative gauge cooling recovery operations to map states back to gauge-invariant subspace.
AI.result: Protocol restores gauge invariance and improves fidelity under depolarizing and amplitude damping noise at rates representative of current superconducting hardware; single-qubit errors are detected by gauge syndrome despite Knill-Laflamme conditions not being generically satisfied.
AI.conclusion: Gauge cooling via syndrome extraction and conditional recovery provides effective active error suppression for quantum simulations of SU(2) lattice gauge theories, compatible with current quantum hardware capabilities.

title: Contrastive learning in tunable dynamical systems
summary: We generalize the theory of supervised contrastive learning, previously applied to physical systems at equilibrium or steady state, to systems following any dynamics described by coupled ordinary differential equations. We show that if physical dynamics break time reversal symmetry, gradient descent on a cost function embodying the desired behavior cannot be achieved with a scalable process, even in principle. We therefore introduce Probably Approximately Right (PAR) learning processes, composed of a local contrastive learning rule and a scalable supervision protocol. We show that approximate, local supervision with forward propagation of the error signal can be used to successfully train several tunable models of physical dynamics inspired by examples in biological and machine learning.

AI.tldr: Generalizes supervised contrastive learning to systems with arbitrary ODE dynamics, shows time-reversal symmetry breaking prevents scalable gradient descent, introduces PAR learning with local contrastive rules and scalable supervision.
AI.motivation: Extend contrastive learning theory beyond equilibrium/steady-state systems to arbitrary dynamical systems described by ODEs, addressing the challenge of training physical systems with broken time-reversal symmetry.
AI.method: Introduces Probably Approximately Right (PAR) learning processes combining local contrastive learning rules with scalable supervision protocols using forward error propagation.
AI.result: Shows that time-reversal symmetry breaking makes scalable gradient descent impossible, but PAR learning successfully trains tunable models of physical dynamics inspired by biological and machine learning examples.
AI.conclusion: PAR learning provides a scalable framework for training dynamical systems with broken time-reversal symmetry, bridging contrastive learning theory with practical applications in physical and biological systems.

title: Non-Relativistic Quantum Mechanics in Multidimensional Geometric Frameworks
summary: A generalized formulation of non-relativistic quantum mechanics is developed within multidimensional geometric (NG) frameworks characterized by a power-law dispersion relation \(E \propto |p|^{j}\), where \(j = N - 1\). Starting from the generalized Minkowski distance in \(L^j\)-normed spaces, the conventional quadratic kinetic structure of three-dimensional geometry is extended to higher-order spatial derivatives, yielding a consistent \(j\)-th order Schrödinger equation. The formalism is applied to free particles and to particles confined within a one-dimensional infinite potential well for 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G geometries. While plane-wave solutions and translational invariance are preserved, the spectral structure is modified, with bound-state energies scaling as \((2n+1)^{j}\), leading to cubic and quartic growth in higher geometries. The corresponding eigenfunctions exhibit mixed exponential, trigonometric, and hyperbolic forms determined by the roots of negative unity. A generalized probability framework based on \(j\)-fold conjugation is introduced, ensuring a real-valued probability density and consistent expectation values. Despite these generalizations, the Heisenberg uncertainty principle is preserved. The formulation presents quantum mechanics as a geometry-dependent theory in which dispersion relations, spectral properties, and probabilistic structure emerge from the underlying spatial metric.

AI.tldr: A generalized formulation of quantum mechanics in multidimensional geometric frameworks with power-law dispersion relations (E ∝ |p|^j), extending conventional quantum mechanics to higher-order spatial derivatives and L^j-normed spaces.
AI.motivation: To develop a geometric foundation for quantum mechanics that extends beyond the conventional quadratic kinetic structure, exploring how different spatial geometries (characterized by power-law dispersion relations) affect quantum mechanical principles and predictions.
AI.method: Starting from generalized Minkowski distance in L^j-normed spaces, extending the quadratic kinetic structure to higher-order spatial derivatives to derive a consistent j-th order Schrödinger equation. Applied to free particles and particles in 1D infinite potential wells for 2G, 3G, 4G, and 5G geometries.
AI.result: Plane-wave solutions and translational invariance are preserved, but spectral structure is modified with bound-state energies scaling as (2n+1)^j (cubic/quartic growth in higher geometries). Eigenfunctions exhibit mixed exponential, trigonometric, and hyperbolic forms. A generalized probability framework based on j-fold conjugation ensures real-valued probability density. The Heisenberg uncertainty principle is preserved despite generalizations.
AI.conclusion: Quantum mechanics can be formulated as a geometry-dependent theory where dispersion relations, spectral properties, and probabilistic structure emerge from the underlying spatial metric, providing a unified geometric framework for generalized quantum mechanics.

title: Skin-Anderson localization transitions in disordered hybrid-nonreciprocal systems
summary: Anderson (localization) transition is a universal wave phenomenon characterized by a disorder-induced quantum phase transition from extended to localized states, whereas the non-Hermitian skin effect is a generic feature of non-Hermitian systems that causes bulk states to localize at the boundaries. Here, we report an unexpected skin-Anderson localization transition arising from the interplay between these two phenomena in hybrid-nonreciprocal systems that exhibit both reciprocity and nonreciprocity in different spatial directions. In the weak-disorder regime, the states are boundary-extended, meaning they are extended in reciprocal spatial dimensions but localized at the boundaries in nonreciprocal dimensions due to the non-Hermitian skin effect. As disorder increases, these boundary-extended states transition to boundary-localized states at a critical disorder strength. Remarkably, the corresponding critical points exhibit universal characteristics akin to those of the Anderson transition in its Hermitian counterpart, including identical critical exponents within numerical errors. When disorder exceeds a higher critical threshold, a second transition occurs in which boundary-localized states become bulk-localized, thereby eliminating the non-Hermitian skin effect. Thus, the skin-Anderson localization transition establishes a new framework for controlling state localization by unifying the physics of Anderson transitions with non-Hermitian topology.

AI.tldr: The paper reports a skin-Anderson localization transition in hybrid-nonreciprocal systems, where interplay between Anderson localization and non-Hermitian skin effect creates three regimes: boundary-extended states at weak disorder, boundary-localized states at intermediate disorder, and bulk-localized states at strong disorder.
AI.motivation: To investigate the interplay between two fundamental wave phenomena: Anderson localization (disorder-induced quantum phase transition) and non-Hermitian skin effect (boundary localization in non-Hermitian systems), particularly in systems with mixed reciprocity/nonreciprocity.
AI.method: Study hybrid-nonreciprocal systems exhibiting both reciprocity and nonreciprocity in different spatial directions, analyze state localization patterns as disorder strength increases, and characterize critical points using numerical methods.
AI.result: Discovery of a three-stage skin-Anderson localization transition: (1) weak disorder: boundary-extended states (extended in reciprocal dimensions, boundary-localized in nonreciprocal dimensions), (2) intermediate disorder: boundary-localized states at critical point with universal characteristics matching Hermitian Anderson transition, (3) strong disorder: bulk-localized states eliminating skin effect.
AI.conclusion: The skin-Anderson localization transition establishes a new framework for controlling state localization by unifying Anderson transition physics with non-Hermitian topology, revealing universal critical behavior and multiple localization regimes.

title: Floquet circuits inspired by holographic matrix models
summary: We argue that near-term experiments with neutral atoms in movable optical tweezers can simulate circuits that mimic the Trotterized time-evolution of simple matrix models in quantum mechanics. As a cartoon of this proposal, we study Floquet Clifford circuits which exhibit a number of signatures of fast scrambling. One such illustration is a simplified Hayden-Preskill recovery protocol, in which stabilizer quantum error correction replaces postselection.

AI.tldr: Neutral atoms in movable optical tweezers can simulate Trotterized time-evolution of simple matrix models, with Floquet Clifford circuits showing fast scrambling signatures and a simplified Hayden-Preskill recovery protocol using stabilizer quantum error correction.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that near-term neutral atom experiments with movable optical tweezers can simulate quantum circuits that mimic Trotterized time-evolution of simple matrix models in quantum mechanics, providing a platform for studying quantum dynamics and scrambling.
AI.method: Use neutral atoms trapped in movable optical tweezers to implement quantum circuits. Study Floquet Clifford circuits as a cartoon model that exhibits fast scrambling signatures. Implement a simplified Hayden-Preskill recovery protocol where stabilizer quantum error correction replaces postselection.
AI.result: The proposal shows that near-term experiments can simulate circuits mimicking Trotterized time-evolution of simple matrix models. Floquet Clifford circuits demonstrate signatures of fast scrambling, and the simplified Hayden-Preskill protocol with stabilizer QEC provides a practical implementation approach.
AI.conclusion: Neutral atom platforms with movable optical tweezers offer a promising near-term experimental approach for simulating quantum dynamics and studying scrambling phenomena, with Floquet Clifford circuits and simplified Hayden-Preskill protocols providing accessible testbeds for these investigations.

title: Magnetic doping-induced second-order and first-order topological phase transition inthe photonic alloy
summary: The bulk-edge correspondence principle, a cornerstone of topological physics, ensures that first-order topological systems host robust chiral edge states in two dimension. This was later extended to higher-order phases, where second-order topological insulators exhibit localized, topologically protected corner states. While the transition between these distinct phases has been demonstrated in periodic systems, its existence in disordered platforms remains an open question. Here, we demonstrate a controllable topological phase transition between a second-order topological phase and a first-order topological phase in a two-dimensional photonic alloy. By tuning the magnetic doping concentration - implemented by attaching permanent magnets randomly to nonmagnetized yttrium iron garnet rods in an alternately magnetized honeycomb lattice with C3 rotational symmetry - we flexibly control the system's topology. At zero doping, we observe higher-order corner states, confirmed by a trivial Chern number and non-zero bulk polarizations of 1/3. As doping concentration increases, these corner states progressively merge with the bulk states, culminating in the closure of the bulk transmission gap. After the bulk transmission gap reopens with further increased doping, the system transitions to a first-order topological phase, characterized by a nontrivial Chern number of -1 and the emergence of a chiral edge state. This transition is reversible, providing a highly tunable and experimentally simple platform for flexibly switching between localized corner states and delocalized chiral edge states within a single photonic system.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of controllable topological phase transition between second-order and first-order topological phases in a 2D photonic alloy via magnetic doping, enabling reversible switching between localized corner states and chiral edge states.
AI.motivation: While topological phase transitions between first-order and second-order phases have been demonstrated in periodic systems, their existence in disordered platforms remains an open question. The paper aims to investigate whether such transitions can occur in disordered systems and provide a tunable platform for switching between different topological phases.
AI.method: Experimental realization using a 2D photonic alloy with C3 rotational symmetry. Magnetic doping concentration is tuned by randomly attaching permanent magnets to nonmagnetized yttrium iron garnet rods in an alternately magnetized honeycomb lattice. Topological properties are characterized through Chern number calculations, bulk polarization measurements, and observation of edge/corner states.
AI.result: At zero doping: higher-order corner states with trivial Chern number (0) and non-zero bulk polarizations (1/3). As doping increases: corner states merge with bulk states, bulk transmission gap closes. After gap reopens at higher doping: first-order topological phase with nontrivial Chern number (-1) and chiral edge states. The transition is reversible.
AI.conclusion: Successfully demonstrated a controllable topological phase transition between second-order and first-order topological phases in a disordered photonic platform. The system provides a highly tunable and experimentally simple platform for flexibly switching between localized corner states and delocalized chiral edge states within a single system.

title: The perturbative method for quantum correlations
summary:
The set $\mathcal{Q}$ of quantum correlations is the collection of all possible probability distributions on measurement outcomes achievable by space-like separated parties sharing a quantum state. Since the original work of Tsirelson [Tsirelson, Lett. Math. Phys. 4, 93 (1980)], this set has mainly been studied through the means algebraic and convex geometry techniques.
  We introduce a perturbative method using Lie-theoretic tools for the unitary group to analyze the response of the evaluations of Bell functionals under infinitesimal unitary perturbations of quantum strategies. Our main result shows that, near classical deterministic points, an $(n, 2, d)$ Bell operator decomposes into a direct sum of $(k, 2, d-1)$ Bell operators which we call \emph{subset games}. We then derive three key insights: (1) in the $(n, 2, 2)$ case, if $p_0$ is classically optimal, it remains locally optimal even among 2-dimensional quantum strategies, implying in turn that the boundary of $\mathcal{Q}$ is flat around classical deterministic points; (2) it suggests a proof strategy for Gisin's open problem on correlations in $\mathcal{Q}(D)$ unattainable by projective strategies of the same dimension; and (3) it establishes that the Ansatz dimension is a critical resource for learning in distributed scenarios, even when the optimal solution admits a low-dimensional representation.

AI.tldr: A perturbative Lie-theoretic method analyzes quantum correlations near classical points, showing Bell operators decompose into subset games and revealing flat boundaries, insights for Gisin's problem, and dimension as critical resource.
AI.motivation: To develop new analytical tools for studying quantum correlation sets beyond traditional algebraic/convex geometry methods, specifically using Lie theory to understand local structure near classical deterministic points.
AI.method: Introduces perturbative Lie-theoretic approach using unitary group tools to analyze Bell functional responses under infinitesimal unitary perturbations; shows decomposition of (n,2,d) Bell operators into direct sum of (k,2,d-1) subset games near classical points.
AI.result: Three key insights: (1) classical optimal points remain locally optimal even among 2D quantum strategies in (n,2,2) case, implying flat boundary of quantum correlation set; (2) suggests proof strategy for Gisin's open problem; (3) establishes Ansatz dimension as critical learning resource in distributed scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Lie-theoretic perturbation theory provides powerful new approach to analyze quantum correlation sets, revealing structural properties near classical points and offering pathways to solve open problems in quantum foundations and distributed learning.

title: Exact Skin Critical Phase and Configurable Fractal Wavefunctions via Imaginary Gauge Phase Imprint in Non-Hermitian Lattices
summary: The generation of complex states like multifractal critical states has been an outstanding challenge in both classical and quantum physics. Here we propose a general framework, termed the imaginary gauge phase imprint, allowing to engineer rigorous wavefunctions in any-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices. Using this method, we uncover a novel phase with exact critical wavefunctions in one (and two) dimension, dubbed the skin critical phase (SCP). Unlike conventional critical phases with overall uniform density distributions and non-Hermitian skin effect with eigenstate accumulation at open boundaries, the SCP is marked by a macroscopically multifractal distribution with all critical eigenstates sharing an identical profile and always accumulating at specific bulk interfaces under periodic boundary condition, which become topology-dependent boundary or interface skin modes under open boundary condition. We also show the ballistic dynamics in the SCP, in contrast to the diffusive behaviour in conventional critical phases. Moreover, we validate our method by imprinting configurable wavefunctions in higher dimensions, including complex fractal states with Sierpinski-carpet and Koch-snowflake profiles in non-fractal lattices and Moire states in non-Moire lattices. Our work not only offers fresh insights into fractal phenomena and critical phases, but also provides a rigorous paradigm for wave manipulations in engineered non-Hermitian systems.

AI.tldr: A framework called "imaginary gauge phase imprint" enables engineering exact wavefunctions in non-Hermitian lattices, revealing a skin critical phase with multifractal distributions and novel critical behavior distinct from conventional phases.
AI.motivation: The generation of complex states like multifractal critical states has been challenging in both classical and quantum physics, creating a need for systematic methods to engineer rigorous wavefunctions in non-Hermitian systems.
AI.method: Proposes "imaginary gauge phase imprint" framework for engineering exact wavefunctions in any-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices, enabling creation of configurable wavefunctions including fractal and Moire states.
AI.result: Uncovers skin critical phase (SCP) with exact critical wavefunctions in 1D and 2D, featuring multifractal distributions, identical eigenstate profiles, topology-dependent skin modes, and ballistic dynamics (vs. diffusive in conventional critical phases).
AI.conclusion: The work provides fresh insights into fractal phenomena and critical phases while establishing a rigorous paradigm for wave manipulation in engineered non-Hermitian systems.

title: Are LLMs Good For Quantum Software, Architecture, and System Design?
summary:
Quantum computers promise massive computational speedup for problems in many critical domains, such as physics, chemistry, cryptanalysis, healthcare, etc. However, despite decades of research, they remain far from entering an era of utility. The lack of mature software, architecture, and systems solutions capable of translating quantum-mechanical properties of algorithms into physical state transformations on qubit devices remains a key factor underlying the slow pace of technological progress. The problem worsens due to significant reliance on domain-specific expertise, especially for software developers, computer architects, and systems engineers. To address these limitations and accelerate large-scale high-performance quantum system design, we ask:
  Can large language models (LLMs) help with solving quantum software, architecture, and systems problems?
  In this work, we present a case study assessing the performance of LLMs on quantum system reasoning tasks. We evaluate nine frontier LLMs and compare their performance to graduate UT Austin students on a set of quantum computing problems. Finally, we recommend several directions along which research and engineering development efforts must be pursued.

AI.tldr: LLMs show promise in quantum computing system design but require specialized development to match human expertise in quantum software, architecture, and systems reasoning.
AI.motivation: Quantum computing progress is hindered by immature software, architecture, and systems solutions, requiring extensive domain expertise. The paper investigates whether LLMs can help bridge this expertise gap and accelerate quantum system design.
AI.method: Case study evaluating nine frontier LLMs on quantum system reasoning tasks, comparing their performance to graduate students at UT Austin on quantum computing problems.
AI.result: LLMs demonstrate potential for assisting with quantum system design tasks, but performance comparison with graduate students reveals specific areas where LLMs excel and where they fall short.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can contribute to solving quantum software, architecture, and systems problems, but targeted research and engineering development are needed to fully leverage their capabilities in this specialized domain.

title: Will a time-varying complex system be stable?
summary: Randomly-assembled dynamical systems are theoretically predicted to be unstable upon crossing a critical threshold of complexity, as first shown by May. Yet, empirical complex systems exhibit remarkable stability, indicating the presence of additional mechanisms playing a stabilizing role. The relation between complexity and stability is typically assessed by assuming fixed interactions, whereas real systems often evolve in intrinsically time-dependent states. To understand how this affects stability, we linearize a general non-autonomous dynamics around a reference operating state and model the resulting parameters as stochastic processes, which represent the minimal extension of static random interactions to time-varying ones. We derive exact stability bounds that generalize complexity-stability theory to dynamically varying systems. Notably, we find that temporal variability allows systems to remain stable even when their instantaneous Jacobian would predict instability. We compare our results against a non-linear neural network model, where our theory applies exactly, and the generalized Lotka-Volterra equations, where we numerically find that time-varying interactions systematically postpone the onset of replica-symmetry breaking. Overall, our results indicate that temporal variability systematically improves stability, demonstrating a general mechanism by which complex systems can violate classical complexity-stability bounds.

AI.tldr: Temporal variability in complex systems allows them to remain stable even when static analysis predicts instability, violating classical complexity-stability bounds.
AI.motivation: Classical complexity-stability theory (May's theorem) predicts instability beyond a critical complexity threshold, but empirical systems remain stable, suggesting missing stabilizing mechanisms. Real systems have time-varying interactions rather than fixed ones.
AI.method: Linearize general non-autonomous dynamics around reference state, model parameters as stochastic processes (minimal extension of static random interactions to time-varying ones). Derive exact stability bounds generalizing complexity-stability theory to dynamically varying systems.
AI.result: Temporal variability allows systems to remain stable even when instantaneous Jacobian predicts instability. Theory applies exactly to nonlinear neural network model. In generalized Lotka-Volterra equations, time-varying interactions systematically postpone replica-symmetry breaking onset.
AI.conclusion: Temporal variability systematically improves stability, providing a general mechanism for complex systems to violate classical complexity-stability bounds.

title: Information-Theoretic Solutions for Seedless QRNG Bootstrapping and Hybrid PQC-QKD Key Combination
summary: This paper considers two challenges faced by practical quantum networks: the bootstrapping of seedless Quantum Random Number Generators (QRNGs) and the resilient combination of Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) keys. These issues are addressed using universal hash functions as strong seeded extractors, with security foundations provided by the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma (QLHL). First, the 'randomness loop' in QRNGs -- the requirement of an initial random seed to generate further randomness -- is resolved by proposing a bootstrapping method using raw data from two independent sources of entropy, given by seedless QRNG sources. Second, it is argued that strong seeded extractors are an alternative to XOR-based key combining that presents different characteristics. Unlike XORing, our method ensures that if the combined output and one initial key are compromised, the remaining key material retains quantifiable min-entropy and remains secure in exchange of longer keys. Furthermore, the proposed method allows to bind transcript information with key material in a natural way, providing a tool to replace computationally based combiners to extend ITS security of the initial key material to the final combined output. By modeling PQC keys as having HILL (Hastad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby) entropy, the framework is extended to hybrid PQC-QKD systems. This unified approach provides a mathematically rigorous and future-proof mechanism for both randomness generation and secure key management against quantum adversaries.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses two quantum network challenges: bootstrapping seedless QRNGs and securely combining PQC and QKD keys using universal hash functions as strong seeded extractors with QLHL security foundations.
AI.motivation: Practical quantum networks face two key challenges: (1) the "randomness loop" problem in QRNGs requiring initial random seeds to generate more randomness, and (2) the need for resilient combination of Post-Quantum Cryptography and Quantum Key Distribution keys against quantum adversaries.
AI.method: Uses universal hash functions as strong seeded extractors based on Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma. For QRNG bootstrapping: combines raw data from two independent seedless entropy sources. For key combining: proposes extractor-based method instead of XOR, allowing transcript binding and preserving min-entropy when one key is compromised. Extends framework to hybrid PQC-QKD systems by modeling PQC keys with HILL entropy.
AI.result: Resolves QRNG randomness loop through bootstrapping from independent entropy sources. Provides alternative to XOR-based key combining that maintains quantifiable min-entropy even when combined output and one initial key are compromised. Enables transcript binding and extends ITS security from initial keys to combined output. Framework supports hybrid PQC-QKD systems.
AI.conclusion: The unified approach using strong seeded extractors provides mathematically rigorous, future-proof mechanisms for both randomness generation and secure key management in quantum networks, addressing bootstrapping and key combination challenges against quantum adversaries.

title: Uncovering the Microscopic Mechanism of Slow Dynamics in Quasiperiodic Many-Body Localized Systems
summary: We study the number entropy and quasiparticle width in one-dimensional quasiperiodic many-body localized (MBL) systems and observe slow dynamics that have previously been investigated in detail only in random systems. In contrast, quasiperiodic systems exhibit more structured growth of both observables. We identify the modulation of the Rabi oscillation amplitude of single-particle hoppings as the mechanism underlying the slow growth even deep in the MBL regime. This quantum amplitude modulation and associated beats arise from the interaction between single-particle hopping processes at different positions in the chain. Interestingly, this mechanism is not weakened by increasing the distance between particles and is generic to many-body quantum systems. We develop an analytical model based on the aforementioned mechanism that explains the observed dynamics at all accessible timescales and provides a microscopic picture of the slow dynamics in the MBL regime. Our results are consistent with the stability of the MBL phase in the thermodynamic limit.

AI.tldr: Study of slow dynamics in quasiperiodic many-body localized systems reveals quantum amplitude modulation of single-particle hoppings as the mechanism for structured growth of number entropy and quasiparticle width, persisting deep in MBL regime.
AI.motivation: To investigate slow dynamics in quasiperiodic many-body localized systems, which have previously been studied mainly in random systems, and understand the underlying mechanisms of structured growth in these systems.
AI.method: Analysis of number entropy and quasiparticle width in one-dimensional quasiperiodic MBL systems, identification of quantum amplitude modulation mechanism from Rabi oscillation amplitude modulation of single-particle hoppings, and development of an analytical model based on interaction between single-particle hopping processes.
AI.result: Quasiperiodic systems exhibit more structured growth of observables compared to random systems. Quantum amplitude modulation and associated beats from interaction between single-particle hopping processes explain slow dynamics even deep in MBL regime, with mechanism not weakened by increasing particle distance. Analytical model explains observed dynamics at all accessible timescales.
AI.conclusion: The quantum amplitude modulation mechanism provides a microscopic picture of slow dynamics in MBL regime, is generic to many-body quantum systems, and results are consistent with stability of MBL phase in thermodynamic limit.

title: Monitoring of quantum walks with weak measurements
summary: Measurements can be used to monitor the evolution of quantum systems and can give rise to quantized return statistics. It is known that the mean return time is quantized for strong monitoring through the winding number of the monitored quantum state. We discuss that under coherent weak monitoring, implemented via ancilla coupling, the mean return time of a quantum walk obeys a scaling relation with respect to the measurement strength. An analog scaling relation was previously found for random-time monitoring, indicating that weak and random-time monitoring have similar effects. We discuss how weak monitoring via ancilla coupling is linked to the unitary evolution, and how this connection can be controlled by a convergent perturbation theory.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how weak quantum monitoring via ancilla coupling affects the mean return time of quantum walks, showing it obeys a scaling relation similar to random-time monitoring.
AI.motivation: To understand how coherent weak monitoring (implemented via ancilla coupling) affects quantum walk dynamics, particularly the mean return time, and to explore connections between weak monitoring and unitary evolution.
AI.method: Uses weak monitoring implemented through ancilla coupling to study quantum walks, analyzes mean return time scaling relations, and develops a convergent perturbation theory to connect weak monitoring to unitary evolution.
AI.result: The mean return time of a quantum walk under weak monitoring obeys a scaling relation with respect to measurement strength, similar to what was previously found for random-time monitoring, indicating comparable effects between these monitoring approaches.
AI.conclusion: Weak monitoring via ancilla coupling produces similar effects on quantum walk dynamics as random-time monitoring, and the connection between weak monitoring and unitary evolution can be systematically controlled through perturbation theory.

title: Thermoforesis from generalized Caldeira-Leggett models
comment: 10 pages, no figures, submitted to Special Issue "Frontiers in Quantum Mechanics and the 45 Years of the Caldeira-Leggett Model", Braz. J. Phys
summary: The standard Caldeira-Leggett model addresses the problem of Brownian motion in a thermal equilibrium environment. Here, we look for generalizations of the Caldeira-Leggett model to account for thermal gradients in the environment. We devise two types of models, and discuss the advantages and limitations of each one. From both models, we find signatures of thermophoresis, i.e., particle transport due to a thermal gradient. In principle, our models can be employed to describe thermophoresis in quantum Brownian particles, an open problem so far.

AI.tldr: Generalization of Caldeira-Leggett model to include thermal gradients, revealing thermophoresis signatures in quantum Brownian motion.
AI.motivation: The standard Caldeira-Leggett model only addresses Brownian motion in thermal equilibrium environments, but real systems often involve thermal gradients. The authors seek to extend this foundational model to account for non-equilibrium thermal environments and study thermophoresis in quantum systems.
AI.method: Developed two types of generalized Caldeira-Leggett models that incorporate thermal gradients in the environment. Analyzed the advantages and limitations of each model approach.
AI.result: Both models reveal signatures of thermophoresis - particle transport driven by thermal gradients. The models provide a framework to describe thermophoresis in quantum Brownian particles, addressing a previously open problem.
AI.conclusion: The proposed generalized Caldeira-Leggett models successfully extend the standard framework to thermal gradient environments, enabling the study of thermophoresis in quantum Brownian systems and opening new avenues for investigating non-equilibrium quantum transport phenomena.

title: Adiabatic dressing of quantum enhanced Markov chains
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures (3 in main text, 6 in appendix)
summary: Quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo, a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm in which configurations are proposed by a quantum proposer and accepted or rejected by a classical algorithm, has been introduced as a possible method for robust quantum speedup. Previous work has identified competing factors that limit the algorithm's performance: the quantum dynamics should delocalize the system across a range of classical states to propose configurations beyond the reach of simple classical updates, whereas excessive delocalization produces configurations unlikely to be accepted, slowing the chain's convergence. Here, we show that controlling the degree of delocalization by adiabatically dressing the quench protocol can significantly enhance the Markov gap in paradigmatic spin-glass models.

AI.tldr: Quantum-enhanced MCMC algorithm uses quantum proposer for configuration generation; controlling delocalization via adiabatic dressing improves Markov gap in spin-glass models.
AI.motivation: Previous quantum-enhanced MCMC algorithms faced competing factors: quantum dynamics need to delocalize enough to propose novel configurations beyond classical reach, but excessive delocalization reduces acceptance rates and slows convergence. The paper aims to address this trade-off.
AI.method: Control the degree of quantum delocalization by adiabatically dressing the quench protocol in quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo. This hybrid approach uses quantum dynamics to propose configurations while classical algorithms handle acceptance/rejection.
AI.result: Adiabatic dressing significantly enhances the Markov gap in paradigmatic spin-glass models, improving algorithm performance by better balancing delocalization and acceptance rates.
AI.conclusion: Controlled delocalization via adiabatic dressing provides an effective strategy to optimize quantum-enhanced MCMC, addressing the fundamental trade-off between exploration (delocalization) and exploitation (acceptance rates) in hybrid quantum-classical algorithms.

title: Hyperbolic Cluster States for Fault-Tolerant Measurement-Based Quantum Computing
summary: Fault-tolerant measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC) provides a compelling framework for fault-tolerant quantum computation, in which quantum information is processed through single-qubit measurements on a three-dimensional entangled resource known as cluster state. To date, this resource has been predominantly studied on Euclidean lattices, most notably in the Raussendorf-Harrington-Goyal (RHG) construction, which underlies topological fault tolerance in MBQC. In this work, we introduce the hyperbolic cluster state, a generalization of the three-dimensional cluster state to negatively curved geometries, obtained via the foliation of periodic hyperbolic lattices. We present an explicit construction of hyperbolic cluster states and investigate their fault-tolerant properties under a realistic circuit-level depolarizing noise model. Using large-scale numerical simulations, we perform memory experiments to characterize their logical error rates and decoding performance. Our results demonstrate that hyperbolic cluster states exhibit a fault-tolerance threshold comparable to that of the Euclidean RHG cluster state, while simultaneously supporting a constant encoding rate in the thermodynamic limit. This represents a substantial improvement in qubit overhead relative to conventional cluster-state constructions. These findings establish hyperbolic geometry as a powerful and experimentally relevant resource for scalable, fault-tolerant MBQC and open new avenues for leveraging negative curvature in quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: Hyperbolic cluster states enable fault-tolerant MBQC with constant encoding rates, reducing qubit overhead compared to Euclidean constructions while maintaining comparable error thresholds.
AI.motivation: Current MBQC relies on Euclidean lattice cluster states (RHG construction), which have limitations in qubit efficiency. The paper aims to explore hyperbolic (negatively curved) geometries as potentially more resource-efficient alternatives for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
AI.method: Construct hyperbolic cluster states via foliation of periodic hyperbolic lattices, then evaluate fault tolerance under circuit-level depolarizing noise using large-scale numerical simulations and memory experiments to measure logical error rates and decoding performance.
AI.result: Hyperbolic cluster states achieve fault-tolerance threshold comparable to Euclidean RHG cluster states while supporting constant encoding rates in the thermodynamic limit, substantially reducing qubit overhead.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic geometry provides a powerful, experimentally relevant resource for scalable fault-tolerant MBQC, opening new avenues for leveraging negative curvature in quantum information processing.

title: Nonunitary Preparation of Nontrivial States from Trivial Regimes in Two-Dimensional Topological Insulators
summary: While remarkable progress has been achieved in engineering nontrivial Hamiltonians across a wide range of physical platforms, preparing their corresponding nontrivial ground states remains a major experimental challenge. The commonly used strategy for state preparation relies on adiabatic protocols. However, when a trivial initial state is unitarily driven toward nontrivial regimes, the dynamics must cross gap-closing critical points, rendering the process intrinsically nonadiabatic, and the state remains topologically trivial. Here, we present a nonunitary method for dynamically preparing nontrivial states in two-dimensional topological insulators. By introducing dephasing noise into a slowly driven unitary evolution, we demonstrate that the topological number of the resulting dephased states can coincide with that of the target nontrivial Hamiltonian. This nearly adiabatic nonunitary state-preparation protocol provides a powerful alternative to conventional adiabatic approaches for accessing topological states.

AI.tldr: Nonunitary state preparation using dephasing noise enables topological ground state preparation in 2D topological insulators despite gap-closing critical points.
AI.motivation: Preparing nontrivial ground states of engineered Hamiltonians remains experimentally challenging because adiabatic protocols fail when crossing gap-closing critical points, leaving states topologically trivial.
AI.method: Introduce dephasing noise into a slowly driven unitary evolution to create a nonunitary state-preparation protocol that can prepare topological states despite critical points.
AI.result: The topological number of dephased states can coincide with that of the target nontrivial Hamiltonian, enabling topological state preparation where unitary adiabatic protocols fail.
AI.conclusion: Nonunitary nearly adiabatic state preparation provides a powerful alternative to conventional adiabatic approaches for accessing topological states in systems with gap-closing critical points.

title: Integrating Julia-ITensors into the Tensor Network Quantum Virtual Machine (TNQVM)
summary: The Tensor Network Quantum Virtual Machine (TNQVM) is a high-performance classical circuit simulation backend for the eXtreme-scale ACCelerator (XACC) framework that leverages the Intelligent Tensor (ITensor) library for tensor network--based quantum circuit simulation. However, TNQVM's original C++ ITensor backend is tied to an older integrated release, limiting access to newer tensor network algorithms, diagnostics, and performance improvements available in the actively developed Julia-based ITensors ecosystem. We introduce JuliaITensorTNQVM, an interoperability layer that bridges TNQVM's C++ visitor infrastructure and the Julia-ITensors runtime through a C-compatible application binary interface. This design preserves the existing XACC/TNQVM programming model while enabling access to modern tensor network capabilities, including entanglement entropy diagnostics exposed directly to XACC. We evaluate the implementation through two studies: a Page-curve verification protocol using Haar-random states, and QAOA MaxCut simulations on 3-regular graphs. Within these tested regimes, results are consistent with expected entanglement behavior and established scaling trends, supporting JuliaITensorTNQVM as a practical modernization path for tensor network simulation in TNQVM.

AI.tldr: JuliaITensorTNQVM bridges TNQVM's C++ infrastructure with Julia-ITensors via C-compatible ABI, enabling access to modern tensor network algorithms while preserving existing XACC/TNQVM programming model.
AI.motivation: TNQVM's original C++ ITensor backend is tied to an older integrated release, limiting access to newer tensor network algorithms, diagnostics, and performance improvements available in the actively developed Julia-based ITensors ecosystem.
AI.method: Created an interoperability layer that bridges TNQVM's C++ visitor infrastructure and the Julia-ITensors runtime through a C-compatible application binary interface, preserving existing XACC/TNQVM programming model while enabling access to modern tensor network capabilities.
AI.result: Implementation evaluated through two studies: Page-curve verification using Haar-random states, and QAOA MaxCut simulations on 3-regular graphs. Results are consistent with expected entanglement behavior and established scaling trends.
AI.conclusion: JuliaITensorTNQVM provides a practical modernization path for tensor network simulation in TNQVM, enabling access to modern tensor network capabilities while maintaining compatibility with existing infrastructure.

title: Derivation of the Schrodinger equation from fundamental principles
summary: Schrodinger path to the quantum mechanical wave equation was heuristic and guided more by physical intuition than formal deduction. Here we derive the Schrodinger equation for the particle wave function, assuming that it has a meaning of the probability amplitude to find the particle at time t at point r and the relations E=hw, p=hk expressing particle energy and momentum in terms of the frequency and wave vector of the associated probability wave.

AI.tldr: Derivation of Schrödinger equation from probability amplitude interpretation and particle-wave relations E=ħω, p=ħk
AI.motivation: Schrödinger's original derivation was heuristic and based on physical intuition rather than formal deduction. The paper aims to provide a more rigorous derivation starting from fundamental quantum mechanical principles.
AI.method: Assume the wave function ψ(r,t) represents the probability amplitude to find a particle at position r at time t. Use the fundamental quantum relations E=ħω and p=ħk connecting particle properties (energy, momentum) to wave properties (frequency, wave vector) of the associated probability wave.
AI.result: The paper derives the time-dependent Schrödinger equation from these basic assumptions, providing a more formal foundation for quantum mechanics.
AI.conclusion: The Schrödinger equation can be systematically derived from the probability amplitude interpretation of the wave function and the fundamental particle-wave relations, offering a more rigorous foundation than Schrödinger's original heuristic approach.

title: Pattern Formation in Quantum Hierarchical Cellular Neural Networks
summary: We present a new class of quantum neural networks (QNNs) whose states are solutions of $p$-adic Schrödinger equations with a non-local potential that controls the interaction between the neurons. These equations are obtained as Wick rotations of the state equations of $p$-adic cellular neural networks (CNNs). The CNNs are continuous limits of discrete hierarchical neural networks (NNs). The CNNs are bio-inspired in the Wilson-Cowan model, which describes the macroscopic dynamics of large populations of neurons. We provide a detailed study of the discretization of the new $p$-adic Schrödinger equations, which allows the construction of new QNNs on simple graphs. We also conduct detailed numerical simulations, offering a clear insight into the functioning of the new QNNs. At a mathematical level, we show the existence of local solutions for the new $p$ -adic Schrödinger equations.

AI.tldr: A new class of quantum neural networks based on p-adic Schrödinger equations derived from hierarchical neural networks, with non-local potentials controlling neuron interactions.
AI.motivation: To develop quantum neural networks that incorporate hierarchical structure and non-local interactions by leveraging p-adic analysis, bridging discrete hierarchical neural networks with quantum formulations.
AI.method: Derive p-adic Schrödinger equations via Wick rotation from state equations of p-adic cellular neural networks, which are continuous limits of discrete hierarchical neural networks. Study discretization for implementation on simple graphs and conduct numerical simulations.
AI.result: Existence of local solutions for p-adic Schrödinger equations proven mathematically. New QNNs constructed on simple graphs through discretization. Numerical simulations provide insight into QNN functioning.
AI.conclusion: A novel framework for quantum neural networks using p-adic analysis successfully bridges hierarchical neural architectures with quantum formulations, enabling new implementations with non-local interactions.

title: Quantum-enhanced estimation of signal field amplitudes with critical squeezed states of photonic modes
summary: Critical phenomena of quantum systems offer a promising strategy to improve measurement precision. So far, many criticality-enhanced quantum metrological schemes have been proposed by using the adiabatically evolved photonic states of composite systems involving a qubit and a field interacting with each other. These schemes focus on the measurement of the system's inherent frequencies. We here propose a criticality-enhanced quantum sensing protocol, aiming to estimate the amplitude of an external signal field with the interacting qubit-photon system. The signal field is coupled to the photonic mode, so that the composite system has a unique dark state, where the photonic mode follows a squeezed vacuum state. The information about the signal field amplitude is encoded in one quadrature of the quantized photonic mode, which exhibits a divergent behavior near the critical point. The measurement precision can approach the Heisenberg limit with respect to the time to encode the signal and the photon number of the field mode.

AI.tldr: Criticality-enhanced quantum sensing protocol using qubit-photon system to estimate external signal field amplitude, achieving Heisenberg-limited precision near critical point.
AI.motivation: Existing criticality-enhanced quantum metrology schemes focus on measuring system's inherent frequencies using adiabatically evolved photonic states. This work aims to extend criticality enhancement to estimate external signal field amplitudes.
AI.method: Proposes a sensing protocol where an external signal field is coupled to the photonic mode of an interacting qubit-photon system. The system has a unique dark state where the photonic mode follows a squeezed vacuum state. Signal amplitude information is encoded in one quadrature of the quantized photonic mode, which exhibits divergent behavior near the critical point.
AI.result: Measurement precision can approach the Heisenberg limit with respect to both the time to encode the signal and the photon number of the field mode, leveraging critical phenomena for enhanced sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: The protocol successfully extends criticality-enhanced quantum metrology to external signal field amplitude estimation, achieving Heisenberg-limited precision by exploiting divergent behavior near critical points in qubit-photon systems.

title: Nonclassical Photon-Bundle Correlations in Quantum Rabi Models
summary: We investigate nonclassical photon-bundle correlations in the quantum Rabi model and its extended cases, using the quantum dressed master equation. By tuning the light--matter coupling strength at finite temperature, the quantum Rabi model exhibits controllable nonclassical transitions between two-photon bundle bunching and antibunching, allowing for the two-photon bundle emission and statistics. We further introduce anisotropic coupling and nonlinear Stark interactions, which enrich the photon statistical behaviors and provide additional tunability of photon-bundle correlations. Extreme correlation behaviors are found to be closely linked to excited-state quantum phase transitions, suggesting a potential pathway for predicting and exploiting excited-state phenomena. These effects can be controlled solely by tuning intrinsic system parameters, without the need for an external modulating field. The quantum Rabi model family thus provides a flexible and experimentally feasible platform for high-purity photon bundle generation and controllable multi-photon sources.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates nonclassical photon-bundle correlations in quantum Rabi models, showing controllable transitions between two-photon bundle bunching and antibunching via coupling strength tuning, with extended models providing additional tunability and connections to excited-state quantum phase transitions.
AI.motivation: To explore and control nonclassical photon-bundle correlations in quantum Rabi systems for generating high-purity photon bundles and controllable multi-photon sources, leveraging intrinsic system parameters without external modulation.
AI.method: Using quantum dressed master equation to analyze quantum Rabi model and its extended cases (anisotropic coupling and nonlinear Stark interactions), tuning light-matter coupling strength at finite temperature.
AI.result: Controllable nonclassical transitions between two-photon bundle bunching and antibunching, enriched photon statistical behaviors with additional tunability, and discovery that extreme correlation behaviors are linked to excited-state quantum phase transitions.
AI.conclusion: The quantum Rabi model family provides a flexible, experimentally feasible platform for high-purity photon bundle generation and controllable multi-photon sources, with potential for predicting and exploiting excited-state phenomena through intrinsic parameter control.

title: Ultralow-power coherent qubit control using AQFP logic at millikelvin temperatures
summary: Qubit controllers are essential for scaling superconducting quantum processors, but implementing them at the 10 mK stage of a dilution refrigerator remains challenging due to stringent cooling constraints. Here we report an ultralow-power qubit controller using adiabatic quantum-flux-parametron (AQFP) logic, termed an AQFP-multiplexed qubit controller with virtual Z gates (AQFP QC-VZ). The AQFP QC-VZ generates multi-tone microwave pulses for qubit control with an ultralow power dissipation of 111 pW per qubit. By combining microwave and time-division multiplexing, the AQFP QC-VZ enables parallel application of X and virtual Z gates to multiple qubits using only a few control lines from room temperature. We demonstrate coherent single-qubit gates at the 10 mK stage using an AQFP mixer, a core component of the AQFP QC-VZ, without observable degradation in coherence.

AI.tldr: Ultralow-power qubit controller using adiabatic quantum-flux-parametron logic achieves 111 pW per qubit power dissipation, enabling multi-qubit control at 10 mK with minimal control lines.
AI.motivation: Qubit controllers at the 10 mK stage of dilution refrigerators face severe cooling constraints, creating a bottleneck for scaling superconducting quantum processors. Existing approaches struggle with power dissipation limitations at cryogenic temperatures.
AI.method: Developed an AQFP-multiplexed qubit controller with virtual Z gates (AQFP QC-VZ) using adiabatic quantum-flux-parametron logic. The system combines microwave and time-division multiplexing to generate multi-tone microwave pulses with ultralow power dissipation. Core component is an AQFP mixer that enables parallel application of X and virtual Z gates to multiple qubits using few control lines.
AI.result: Achieved ultralow power dissipation of 111 pW per qubit. Demonstrated coherent single-qubit gates at 10 mK stage without observable degradation in qubit coherence. The system enables parallel control of multiple qubits with minimal room-temperature control lines.
AI.conclusion: The AQFP QC-VZ represents a significant advancement for cryogenic qubit control, solving the power dissipation challenge at 10 mK while maintaining qubit coherence. This enables scalable quantum processor control with minimal thermal load.

title: From Foundation ECG Models to NISQ Learners: Distilling ECGFounder into a VQC Student
summary: Foundation models have recently improved electrocardiogram (ECG) representation learning, but their deployment can be limited by computational cost and latency constraints. In this work, we fine-tune ECGFounder as a high-capacity teacher for binary ECG classification on PTB-XL and the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, and investigate whether knowledge distillation can transfer its predictive behavior to compact students. We evaluate two classical 1D students (ResNet-1D and a lightweight CNN-1D) and a quantum-ready pipeline that combines a convolutional autoencoder, which compresses 256-sample ECG windows into a low-dimensional latent representation, with a 6-qubit variational quantum circuit implemented in Qiskit and executed in a simulated backend. Across both datasets, the teacher provides the strongest overall performance, while distillation yields competitive students under a considerable reduction in trainable parameters. We further analyze the sensitivity of student performance to distillation settings, highlighting consistent accuracy--efficiency trade-offs when compressing a foundation ECG model into classical and quantum-ready learners under a unified evaluation protocol.

AI.tldr: Knowledge distillation transfers ECG classification performance from a high-capacity foundation model teacher to compact classical and quantum-ready student models, achieving competitive accuracy with significantly reduced parameters.
AI.motivation: Foundation models for ECG analysis face deployment limitations due to computational cost and latency constraints, necessitating more efficient models that can maintain performance while being suitable for resource-constrained environments.
AI.method: Fine-tune ECGFounder as teacher for binary ECG classification on PTB-XL and MIT-BIH datasets, then use knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge to: 1) classical 1D students (ResNet-1D and lightweight CNN-1D), and 2) quantum-ready pipeline combining convolutional autoencoder for compression with 6-qubit variational quantum circuit implemented in Qiskit.
AI.result: Teacher provides strongest overall performance, while distillation yields competitive students with considerable reduction in trainable parameters. Analysis reveals consistent accuracy-efficiency trade-offs when compressing foundation ECG models into classical and quantum-ready learners.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge distillation effectively transfers predictive behavior from high-capacity ECG foundation models to compact students, enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings while maintaining competitive performance, with consistent trade-offs observed across classical and quantum-ready architectures.

title: Quantum Bit Error Rate Analysis in BB84 Quantum Key Distribution: Measurement, Statistical Estimation, and Eavesdropping Detection
summary: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) provides information-theoretic security by exploiting the principles of quantum mechanics. Among QKD protocols, the BB84 scheme remains the most widely adopted for both theoretical research and practical implementation. A critical parameter determining the reliability and security of BB84 is the Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), which quantifies errors in the sifted key arising from channel noise or potential eavesdropping. This paper presents a systematic review and analysis of QBER within the BB84 protocol, examining its calculation, statistical estimation methods, and role in detecting eavesdropping activity. Simulation results, corroborated by reported experimental observations, reveal a near-linear relationship between eavesdropping intensity and QBER, with values approaching 25% under full intercept-resend attacks. Four confidence interval estimation methods, Wald, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and Hoeffding's inequality, are compared for robust QBER analysis in finite-key scenarios. Protocol enhancements, including decoy-state methods, hybrid cryptographic models, and quantum-resistant authentication, are discussed as mechanisms to mitigate errors and strengthen resilience across fiber, free-space, underwater, and satellite QKD systems. Open challenges in distinguishing noise-induced errors from malicious eavesdropping, and the role of adaptive error correction and machine-learning-assisted QBER estimation in future quantum networks, are identified as key directions for further research.

AI.tldr: Systematic review of Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) in BB84 QKD protocol, analyzing calculation methods, statistical estimation, eavesdropping detection, and mitigation techniques across various QKD systems.
AI.motivation: QBER is a critical parameter determining reliability and security of BB84 QKD, but requires systematic analysis of its calculation, statistical estimation, and role in eavesdropping detection for practical implementation.
AI.method: Systematic review and analysis of QBER in BB84 protocol, including simulation studies, comparison of four confidence interval estimation methods (Wald, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, Hoeffding's inequality), and examination of protocol enhancements.
AI.result: Simulation results show near-linear relationship between eavesdropping intensity and QBER, with values approaching 25% under full intercept-resend attacks. Statistical methods comparison provides robust QBER analysis for finite-key scenarios.
AI.conclusion: QBER analysis is essential for BB84 security assessment, with protocol enhancements (decoy-state methods, hybrid models, quantum-resistant authentication) improving resilience. Future research should address noise-eavesdropping distinction and adaptive error correction with ML-assisted estimation.

title: NNQA: Neural-Native Quantum Arithmetic for End-to-End Polynomial Synthesis
summary: Hybrid classical quantum learning is often bottlenecked by communication overhead and approximation error from generic variational ansatzes. In this study, we introduce Neural Native Quantum Arithmetic (NNQA), which compiles classically learned nonlinear representations into precise quantum arithmetic composed of native unitary blocks. Theoretically, we prove that the universal approximation of quantum polynomial arithmetic can be realized by transforming a classical neural network into a quantum circuit, with the resulting error arising solely from measurement shot noise, thereby extending classical operator-level estimation guarantees into the quantum regime. Empirical validation on IBM Quantum Heron3 and IonQ Forte processors shows performance limited primarily by device noise without variational fine tuning: we achieve over 99.5% accuracy for polynomials up to degree 35 and demonstrate scalability on IonQ hardware up to 36 qubits and circuit depths of 70, reaching a negligible RMSE of 0.005. Overall, NNQA establishes a new paradigm of synthesizing quantum arithmetic for native quantum computation.

AI.tldr: NNQA compiles classical neural networks into precise quantum arithmetic circuits using native unitary blocks, eliminating variational optimization overhead and achieving high accuracy on quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Hybrid classical-quantum learning faces bottlenecks from communication overhead and approximation errors from generic variational ansatzes. There's a need for precise quantum arithmetic compilation that avoids variational fine-tuning.
AI.method: Neural Native Quantum Arithmetic (NNQA) compiles classically learned nonlinear representations into precise quantum arithmetic composed of native unitary blocks. It transforms classical neural networks into quantum circuits, with error arising only from measurement shot noise.
AI.result: On IBM Quantum Heron3 and IonQ Forte processors: achieved over 99.5% accuracy for polynomials up to degree 35; demonstrated scalability on IonQ hardware up to 36 qubits and circuit depths of 70; reached negligible RMSE of 0.005; performance limited primarily by device noise without variational fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: NNQA establishes a new paradigm for synthesizing quantum arithmetic for native quantum computation, extending classical operator-level estimation guarantees into the quantum regime with theoretical error bounds limited to measurement shot noise.

title: Time of arrival on a ring and relativistic quantum clocks
summary: We study the time-of-arrival problem for relativistic particles constrained to move on a ring, formulating the problem entirely within Quantum Field Theory (QFT). In contrast to its counterpart for motion in a line, the circle topology implies that particles may encounter the detector multiple times before detection, making a field-theoretic treatment of the measurement interaction essential. We employ the Quantum Temporal Probabilities (QTP) method to derive a class of Positive-Operator-Valued Measures (POVMs) for time-of-arrival observables directly from QFT. We analyze the resulting detection probabilities in both semiclassical and fully quantum regimes, identifying the relevant timescales and their dependence on the field-theoretic parameters. For ensembles of particles, the detection signal is a periodic function, providing a realization of a quantum clock whose operation reflects the local spacetime structure. We also extend the formalism to rotating rings and show that rotation induces additional noise in detection probabilities, interpretable as a manifestation of the rotational Unruh effect. Finally, we investigate multi-time measurements and demonstrate the emergence of non-classical temporal correlations due to entanglement.

AI.tldr: Relativistic QFT formulation of time-of-arrival measurements on a ring using Quantum Temporal Probabilities method, yielding periodic detection signals that function as quantum clocks, with extensions to rotating rings showing rotational Unruh effect and multi-time measurements revealing non-classical temporal correlations.
AI.motivation: To address the time-of-arrival problem for relativistic particles constrained to move on a ring, which differs fundamentally from linear motion due to the circular topology allowing particles to encounter detectors multiple times before detection, necessitating a field-theoretic treatment of measurement interactions.
AI.method: Employ the Quantum Temporal Probabilities (QTP) method to derive Positive-Operator-Valued Measures (POVMs) for time-of-arrival observables directly from Quantum Field Theory, analyzing detection probabilities in semiclassical and fully quantum regimes, and extending to rotating rings and multi-time measurements.
AI.result: Derived a class of POVMs for time-of-arrival observables; detection probabilities show periodic signals functioning as quantum clocks reflecting local spacetime structure; rotation induces additional noise interpretable as rotational Unruh effect; multi-time measurements demonstrate emergence of non-classical temporal correlations due to entanglement.
AI.conclusion: The QFT-based approach successfully addresses the time-of-arrival problem on rings, revealing fundamental connections between quantum measurement theory, relativistic field theory, and spacetime structure, with implications for quantum clocks, rotational Unruh effects, and quantum temporal correlations.

title: Single-photon-boosted type-I fusion gates
summary: Fusion measurements are a key primitive for linear-optical quantum computing and quantum networks. Type-I and type-II fusion gates are widely used to combine small entangled resource states into larger photonic states, but without ancillary resources their success probability is limited to $1/2$. Existing $3/4$-efficient type-I schemes rely on entangled Bell-pair ancillary states, whose preparation is itself probabilistic and resource-intensive. Here we propose a boosted type-I fusion gate that achieves a total success probability of $3/4$ using only four ancillary single photons and passive linear optics. The gate succeeds directly with probability $5/8$, while a distillation step converts partially entangled outcomes into additional successful events. We quantify the practical advantage of this scheme by estimating the photonic resources required for generating representative large entangled photonic states and show that the proposed gate significantly reduces the required overhead. These results expand the set of resource-efficient linear-optical primitives and enable a substantial reduction in the resource requirements for scalable photonic quantum computing and quantum communication.

AI.tldr: Proposes a boosted type-I fusion gate achieving 3/4 success probability using only four ancillary single photons and passive linear optics, significantly reducing resource overhead for photonic quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Existing type-I fusion gates have limited success probability (1/2) without ancillary resources, and 3/4-efficient schemes require entangled Bell-pair ancillary states that are themselves probabilistic and resource-intensive to prepare.
AI.method: Proposes a boosted type-I fusion gate using four ancillary single photons and passive linear optics. The gate succeeds directly with probability 5/8, with a distillation step converting partially entangled outcomes into additional successful events.
AI.result: Achieves total success probability of 3/4, significantly reduces photonic resource requirements for generating large entangled photonic states compared to existing schemes.
AI.conclusion: Expands resource-efficient linear-optical primitives and enables substantial reduction in resource requirements for scalable photonic quantum computing and quantum communication.

title: Quantum Conditional Stochastic Processes
summary: Quantum mechanics contains some strange unphysical concepts. Among these are complex numbers, Hilbert spaces with their unitary and self-adjoint operators, states represented by complex vectors, superpositions of states, collapse of wave functions, Born's rule for probabilities and others. If we accept that quantum mechanics is probabilistic, then these concepts can be derived and they become secondary. In this work, we begin with what we call a \textit{conditional stochastic process} (CSP) which is based on real numbers and probabilities. As we shall see, such processes are defined by three simple axioms. We then use CSP to derive quantum mechanics by employing a correspondence called a \textit{dictionary}. We also show that the converse holds. That is, beginning with a quantum system, we employ the dictionary to derive a CSP.
