Here, by leveraging advances in high-rate quantum error-correcting codes, efficient logical instruction sets, and circuit design, we show that Shor's algorithm can be executed at cryptographically relevant scales with as few as 10,000 reconfigurable atomic qubits. Increasing the number of physical qubits improves time efficiency by enabling greater parallelism; under plausible assumptions, the runtime for discrete logarithms on the P-256 elliptic curve could be just a few days for a system with 26,000 physical qubits, while the runtime for factoring RSA-2048 integers is one to two orders of magnitude longer. Recent neutral-atom experiments have demonstrated universal fault-tolerant operations below the error-correction threshold, computation on arrays of hundreds of qubits, and trapping arrays with more than 6,000 highly coherent qubits. Although substantial engineering challenges remain, our theoretical analysis indicates that an appropriately designed neutral-atom architecture could support quantum computation at cryptographically relevant scales. More broadly, these results highlight the capability of neutral atoms for fault-tolerant quantum computing with wide-ranging scientific and technological applications.

AI.tldr: Shor's algorithm for cryptography can be executed with only 10,000 atomic qubits using optimized quantum error correction and circuit design, significantly reducing resource requirements from millions to thousands of qubits.
AI.motivation: Current quantum error correction overhead requires millions of physical qubits for cryptographically relevant instances of Shor's algorithm, creating a major barrier to practical implementation. The paper aims to dramatically reduce these resource requirements.
AI.method: Leverages advances in high-rate quantum error-correcting codes, efficient logical instruction sets, and optimized circuit design for Shor's algorithm, specifically targeting neutral-atom architectures with reconfigurable atomic qubits.
AI.result: Shor's algorithm can be executed with as few as 10,000 reconfigurable atomic qubits. With 26,000 qubits, discrete logarithms on P-256 elliptic curve could run in days, while RSA-2048 factoring would take 1-2 orders of magnitude longer. Recent experiments demonstrate key building blocks: fault-tolerant operations below threshold, computation on hundreds of qubits, and trapping arrays with >6,000 coherent qubits.
AI.conclusion: Neutral-atom architectures could support quantum computation at cryptographically relevant scales with substantially reduced resource requirements, highlighting their potential for fault-tolerant quantum computing with broad scientific and technological applications.

title: Qubit-efficient embedding of parity-encoded Hamiltonians in quantum annealers
summary: The Sourlas-Lechner-Hauke-Zoller (SLHZ) scheme for quantum annealing uses the parity to encode logical variables and has several advantages, but it has not been implemented for large-scale quantum annealers. If the SLHZ-based approach can be implemented on currently available quantum annealers, we can evaluate its performance. An efficient method to embed the parity-encoded model into the hardware graphs of available quantum annealers is one of the key elements for this approach. We propose a qubit-efficient embedding scheme for parity-encoded Hamiltonians on quantum annealers with the Zephyr connectivity. We give an explicit constructive embedding of the interaction graph of an intermediate Hamiltonian, which contains only one- and two-body interactions, into the Zephyr graph. Our embedding maps each spin to a two-qubit chain using systematic chain-assignment rules. Its validity is verified via the resulting chain-to-chain connectivity. Our embedding also offers practical flexibility. Chains assigned to ancillary spins allow reduction to a single physical qubit, leading to options to avoid inactive qubits. The number of required qubits per spin in the parity Hamiltonian is three, which is fewer than that for a known embedding scheme for the Pegasus graph.

AI.tldr: Proposes a qubit-efficient embedding scheme for parity-encoded Hamiltonians on quantum annealers with Zephyr connectivity, requiring only 3 qubits per spin.
AI.motivation: The SLHZ scheme for quantum annealing has advantages but hasn't been implemented on large-scale quantum annealers. An efficient embedding method is needed to implement parity-encoded models on available hardware.
AI.method: Proposes embedding scheme that maps each spin to a two-qubit chain using systematic chain-assignment rules. Explicit constructive embedding of interaction graph into Zephyr graph, with flexibility to reduce ancillary spins to single physical qubits.
AI.result: Valid embedding scheme requiring only 3 qubits per spin in parity Hamiltonian, fewer than known embedding for Pegasus graph. Offers practical flexibility to avoid inactive qubits.
AI.conclusion: Provides efficient embedding method enabling implementation of SLHZ-based quantum annealing on current Zephyr-architecture quantum annealers.

title: Efficient and Practical Black-Box Verification of Quantum Metric Learning Algorithms
comment: International Conference on Quantum Communications, Networking, and Computing (QCNC 2026)
summary: Quantum metric learning enhances machine learning by mapping classical data to a quantum Hilbert space with maximal separation between classes. However, on current NISQ hardware, this mapping process itself is prone to errors and could be fundamentally incorrect. Verifying that a quantum embedding model successfully achieves its promised separation is essential to ensure the correctness and reliability. In this paper, we propose a practical black-box verification protocol to audit the performance of quantum metric learning models. We define a setting with two parties: a powerful but untrusted prover, who claims to have a parameterized unitary circuit that embeds classical data from different groups with a guaranteed angular separation, and a limited verifier, whose quantum capabilities are restricted to performing only basic measurements. The verifier has no knowledge of the implementation of the prover, including the structure of the model, its parameters, or the details of the prover measurement setup. To verify the separation between different data groups, the proposed algorithm must overcome two key challenges. First, the verifier is ignorant of the prover's implementation details, such as the optimization cost function and measurement setup. Consequently, the verifier lacks any prior information about the expected quantum embedding states for each group. Second, the destructive nature of quantum measurements prevents direct estimation of the separation angles. Our algorithm successfully overcomes these challenges, enabling the verifier to accurately estimate the true separation angles between the different groups. We implemented the proposed protocol and deployed it to verify the QAOAEmbedding models. The results from both theoretical analysis and practical implementation show that our proposal effectively assesses embedding quality and remains robust in adversarial settings.

AI.tldr: Proposes a black-box verification protocol for quantum metric learning models to audit class separation in quantum embeddings without requiring knowledge of model implementation details.
AI.motivation: Quantum metric learning on NISQ hardware is prone to errors, making verification of promised class separation essential for correctness and reliability of quantum embedding models.
AI.method: Black-box verification protocol with two parties: untrusted prover with parameterized unitary circuit, and limited verifier with only basic measurement capabilities. Algorithm overcomes challenges of implementation ignorance and destructive quantum measurements.
AI.result: Protocol successfully enables verifier to estimate true separation angles between different data groups. Implementation verifies QAOAEmbedding models, showing effective assessment of embedding quality and robustness in adversarial settings.
AI.conclusion: Proposed practical verification protocol addresses critical need for auditing quantum metric learning models, overcoming key challenges to ensure reliable quantum embeddings on NISQ hardware.

title: Modeling Quantum Optomechanical STIRAP
summary: Quantum optomechanical STIRAP (Stimulated Raman Adiabatic Passage) is investigated for a system of two mechanical modes coupled to an optical mode. We show analytically that in a system without loss, fractional STIRAP can generate a mechanical Bell state from a single phonon Fock state of one of the mechanical modes with the other mechanical mode in the vacuum state, and a product state from a coherent state. Relative phases between Fock basis components in the final state of STIRAP are determined by the phonon-number parity of the initial state. Furthermore, the system is numerically studied to determine the effects of dissipation, and it is concluded that high-fidelity entanglement can be achieved via fractional STIRAP using state-of-the-art cryogenic cooling and mechanical devices. Finally, an interferometric protocol using time-reversed fractional STIRAP is proposed to quantify entanglement between two mechanical modes.

AI.tldr: Quantum optomechanical STIRAP enables mechanical Bell state generation from single phonon Fock states and coherent states, with entanglement robust to dissipation and measurable via time-reversed protocols.
AI.motivation: To develop quantum control techniques for mechanical systems using STIRAP to generate and quantify entanglement between mechanical modes in optomechanical systems.
AI.method: Analytical study of lossless quantum optomechanical STIRAP for two mechanical modes coupled to an optical mode, followed by numerical investigation of dissipation effects, and proposal of interferometric protocol using time-reversed fractional STIRAP.
AI.result: Fractional STIRAP can generate mechanical Bell states from single phonon Fock states and product states from coherent states; relative phases depend on phonon-number parity; high-fidelity entanglement achievable with state-of-the-art cryogenic cooling; time-reversed protocol enables entanglement quantification.
AI.conclusion: Quantum optomechanical STIRAP provides a viable method for generating and quantifying mechanical entanglement, with practical feasibility demonstrated through numerical simulations accounting for realistic dissipation.

title: Construction and characterization of measures in block coherence resource theory
summary: Quantum coherence, as a direct manifestation of the quantum superposition principle, is a crucial resource in quantum information processing. Block coherence resource theory generalizes the traditional coherence framework by defining coherence via a set of orthogonal projectors. Within this framework, we investigates the construction and comparison of block coherence measures. First, we propose two universal methods for constructing coherence measures and introduce a two-parameter family of measures based on the $α$-$z$ Rényi relative entropy and a family of measures based on the Tsallis relative operator entropy. Second, through theoretical proofs and numerical counterexamples, we compares the ordering relations and numerical magnitudes among different block coherence measures and establishes a series of universal numerical inequalities to constrain their values. Besides, we also use $C_{α,1}$ to show the role of coherence in complex dynamic evolution of the Kominis master equation that includes recombination reactions.
